guides.title: How Long to Cook a Burger (Stove, Grill & Oven Times)
guides.excerpt: Cook a 1-inch beef burger 6 to 10 minutes on the stove, 15 to 17 minutes in a 400F oven, or about 10 minutes on the grill to a USDA-safe 160F internal temperature.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-08-09.

Cook a burger 6 to 10 minutes on the stove, 15 to 17 minutes in a 400°F oven, or about 10 minutes on the grill

For a standard 1-inch, 80/20 beef patty, that means roughly 3 to 5 minutes per side on the stovetop, 15 to 17 minutes unflipped in the oven at 400°F, or checking a grill burger at the 10- to 15-minute mark the USDA recommends. The only real finish line is internal temperature: ground beef is safe at 160°F (FSIS). Set an 8-minute timer for medium stovetop burgers, a 10-minute timer for well-done or a grill check, or a 12-minute timer as an oven midpoint.

Why 160°F matters more than minutes

Ground beef carries more risk than a whole steak because grinding spreads surface bacteria throughout the meat. The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service requires all raw ground beef, pork, lamb, and veal to reach a safe minimum internal temperature of 160°F, measured with a food thermometer (FSIS Ground Beef and Food Safety). Color is not a reliable signal: USDA research found roughly 1 in 4 hamburgers turns brown before it reaches a safe temperature (FSIS, Is It Done Yet?). Treat the minutes below as a planning tool and the thermometer as the verdict. If you're cooking poultry patties instead, see our grill chicken guide — ground poultry needs 165°F.

Cooking times by method and doneness

Times assume a 1-inch-thick patty formed from 80% lean ground beef. Thicker patties, colder meat, and leaner blends all add time.

MethodHeatTimeSafe finish
Stovetop skilletMedium-high~8 min (medium) to 10 min (well-done); 3–5 min per side160°F
Oven bake (no flip)400°F15–17 min (~140°F at 15 min = medium, still below safe)160°F
GrillMedium (~350–400°F)~4–5 min per side; check at 10–15 min160°F
Turkey / chicken burgerAnyAdd ~1–2 min per side vs. beef165°F

Stovetop doneness benchmarks run medium-rare at about 6 minutes total, medium at 7 to 8 minutes, medium-well at 9 minutes, and well-done at 10 minutes (The Kitchn). For an oven burger on a wire rack at 400°F, 15 minutes lands around 140°F (medium) and 17 minutes pushes it toward well-done (The Kitchn). On the grill, the USDA specifically advises checking each burger with a food thermometer after roughly 10 to 15 minutes of total cooking (FSIS, Is It Done Yet?).

How to cook a burger on the stove

  1. Use 80% lean ground beef; anything leaner than 90% tends to dry out and crumble (The Kitchn).
  2. Form 1-inch patties gently — overworking the meat makes it tough — and press a shallow dimple in the center so they stay flat instead of doming.
  3. Heat a skillet or griddle over medium-high until you see the first wisp of smoke, then add the patties.
  4. Cook 3 to 4 minutes, flip once, then cook another 3 to 5 minutes to your preferred doneness. Add cheese right after the flip and cover briefly to melt.
  5. Verify 160°F with a thermometer before serving (FSIS).

Set an 8-minute timer for medium patties and a 10-minute timer for well-done. Use a thin spatula and flip only once to keep the crust intact.

Grill and oven methods

On the grill: Preheat to medium (roughly 350–400°F). Grill burgers about 4 to 5 minutes per side, flipping once, and the USDA requires ground meats to reach 160°F on the grill just as they do indoors (FSIS, Food Safety Belongs on the Grill). A 10-minute timer is the right moment for that first temperature check. Building a full cookout? Our grill chicken timing pairs well on the same fire.

In the oven: Heat to 400°F and set patties on a wire rack over a foil-lined baking sheet so heat circulates underneath — no flipping needed. Bake 15 to 17 minutes; at 15 minutes a patty sits around 140°F (medium), which is still below the USDA safe minimum, so continue to 17 minutes or until a thermometer reads 160°F (The Kitchn; FSIS). Add cheese in the final minute and toast the buns on a separate rack for the last 5 to 6 minutes. A 12-minute timer marks the midpoint, when you should start watching closely.

Food safety, handling, and troubleshooting

Refrigerate ground beef at 40°F or below and cook or freeze it within 1 to 2 days. Keep raw and cooked items separate, and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours — 1 hour if the air temperature is above 90°F (FSIS). Safe minimum internal temperatures: whole beef, pork, veal, and lamb steaks and roasts 145°F with a 3-minute rest; all ground meats 160°F; all poultry 165°F (FSIS Safe Minimum Internal Temperature Chart). For a breakfast side, our bacon timing guide covers the safe-crisp window.

Quick fixes for common problems: dry, dense patties come from overworking the meat or using too-lean beef, so handle the beef gently and stick to 80/20; domed centers are prevented by the dimple trick; brown outside but undercooked inside means the heat is too high — drop to medium and trust the thermometer, since 1 in 4 burgers browns before it is actually safe (FSIS).

guides.title: How Long to Cook Quinoa (Stovetop & Rice Cooker Times)
guides.excerpt: Cook quinoa 15 minutes on the stovetop for white (20 for black) at a 1:2 quinoa-to-water ratio, then rest covered 10 minutes. A rice cooker finishes it on the white-rice cycle in 15-20 minutes. One cup dry yields about 3 cups cooked.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-08-09.

How long to cook quinoa: the short answer

Cook quinoa on the stovetop for 15 minutes for white (pearl) quinoa, 18 minutes for red, and 20 minutes for black, using a 1:2 ratio of quinoa to liquid (1 cup dry quinoa to 2 cups water or broth) and finishing with a 10-minute covered rest off the heat. In a rice cooker, the white-rice cycle takes about 15-20 minutes. One cup of dry quinoa yields roughly 3 cups cooked.

The stovetop method, step by step

The reliable stovetop method is the same one Michigan State University Extension publishes: a 1:2 quinoa-to-liquid ratio, a quick boil, then a covered simmer until the liquid is absorbed and the grain is soft. Here is the precise sequence:

  1. Rinse 1 cup of quinoa in a fine-mesh strainer under cold water for 30-60 seconds. Quinoa's seed coat is coated in saponins, bitter compounds that taste soapy if you skip this step.
  2. Combine the rinsed, drained quinoa with 2 cups of water or broth and a pinch of salt in a saucepan.
  3. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat (about 3-4 minutes).
  4. Cover and reduce to a low simmer. Set a 15-minute timer for white quinoa (18 for red, 20 for black and tri-color blends).
  5. Rest covered for 10 minutes off the heat after the timer goes off. This is the step that turns out fluffy grain rather than a wet mess according to Foolproof Living's tested ratios.
  6. Fluff with a fork and serve.

Cooking times by quinoa type and method

Cooking time tracks the color of the seed: darker quinoa has a tougher outer layer and needs a few extra minutes. The liquid ratio and yield stay constant across all types. The per-color simmer times below match Foolproof Living's kitchen testing of white, red, black, and tri-color quinoa.

Quinoa typeLiquid per 1 cup drySimmer timeCovered restApprox. yield
White (pearl)2 cups15 min10 min~3 cups
Red2 cups18 min10 min~3 cups
Black2 cups20 min10 min~3 cups
Tri-color blend2 cups18-20 min10 min~3 cups
Rice cooker (any type)2 cups15-20 min (white-rice cycle)5 min natural~3 cups

Variables that change your result

Water ratio. The 1:2 ratio is the safe default and what MSU Extension uses. If you want firmer, separate grains for a salad, drop to about 1 3/4 cups liquid per 1 cup quinoa (the drier ratio that Foolproof Living tested head-to-head against 1:2 and found only minimally different); for soft, porridge-like quinoa, push toward 2 cups plus 2 tablespoons of liquid per 1 cup quinoa.

Rinsing. Most U.S. supermarket quinoa is pre-rinsed, but the package rarely says so plainly. Rinsing for under a minute removes residual saponin and any grit, and it is free insurance against bitterness.

The 10-minute rest. Skipping the rest leaves moisture still migrating through the seed. Covered and off the heat, the grain finishes steaming in its own residual heat and the last liquid absorbs without scorching.

Quinoa cooks much like other pantry grains. For comparison, see our guides on how long to cook rice and how long to cook oatmeal.

How to cook quinoa in a rice cooker

A rice cooker is the lowest-effort path because it handles the boil-simmer-switch-off automatically. Use the same 1:2 ratio (1 cup rinsed quinoa to 2 cups liquid), add salt, and run the white-rice cycle, which on most machines lasts about 15-20 minutes. Let it sit for 5 minutes after the cycle clicks off, then fluff. Red and black quinoa may need a couple of extra minutes on the same setting; if the machine shuts off and liquid remains, run a second short cycle.

Food safety and storage

Quinoa is a low-moisture dry grain, so the food-safety concerns arrive after cooking. The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service places cooked foods in the danger zone between 40 and 140 F, where bacteria multiply fastest per FSIS leftovers guidance. Follow three rules:

  • Refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking (1 hour if the room is above 90 F).
  • Store cooked quinoa 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator at 40 F or below, or freeze for 3 to 4 months.
  • Reheat leftovers to 165 F, measured with a food thermometer. This is the same 165 F internal minimum FSIS sets for poultry, and it applies to reheated grain dishes and casseroles built on quinoa.

Troubleshooting: mushy, bitter, or crunchy quinoa

Mushy quinoa. Cause: too much liquid or too long on the heat. Fix: drain any pooled water, spread the quinoa on a sheet pan uncovered for 10 minutes so the surface dries, then fluff. Next time, measure the liquid precisely and do not lift the lid during the simmer.

Bitter quinoa. Cause: unrinsed saponin. Fix: rinse the raw grain longer (60-90 seconds) before cooking. If a cooked batch still tastes soapy, fold in a squeeze of lemon or a pinch of sugar to mask it, and rinse the next batch more thoroughly.

Crunchy or undercooked quinoa. Cause: not enough liquid, heat too low to maintain a simmer, or the lid was off. Fix: add 2-3 tablespoons of boiling water, cover, and cook another 3-5 minutes until the white germ spirals (the little "tail") release and the grain is tender.

guides.title: How Long to Bake Cookies (Time & Temperature Chart)
guides.excerpt: Most cookies bake at 350°F for 9 to 12 minutes. Use this time-and-temperature chart by type — chocolate chip, sugar, oatmeal, cut-out, shortbread, and bars — plus egg-and-flour safety temps.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-08-09.

Most cookies bake at 350°F for 9 to 12 minutes

Bake standard drop cookies — chocolate chip, sugar, and oatmeal — at 350°F (175°C) for 9 to 12 minutes, until the edges are golden and the centers still look a touch underdone. Small or thin cookies finish at 9 minutes; large, chewy ones need 11 to 12. Cut-out sugar cookies bake at 375°F (190°C) for 8 to 10 minutes, and cookie bars in an 11×7 dish take 375°F for 15 to 18 minutes. Cookies keep cooking on the hot pan after it leaves the oven, so pull them early.

Cookie baking time and temperature chart

Times assume a fully preheated oven, dough portioned at 2 tablespoons, and a light-colored half-sheet pan lined with parchment. Start checking two minutes before the low end of every range.

Cookie typeOven tempBake timeDone when…
Chocolate chip (2-tbsp drop)350°F (175°C)10–12 min — set an 11-minute timerEdges golden, center pale and soft
Small / mini drop cookies350°F (175°C)8–10 minTops crackle, edges just set
Drop sugar cookies350°F (175°C)8–10 minEdges lightly golden
Oatmeal cookies350°F (175°C)10–12 min — try a 12-minute timerEdges set, tops no longer wet
Cut-out / rolled sugar cookies375°F (190°C)8–10 min — set a 9-minute timerEdges barely starting to color
Shortbread350°F (175°C)12–15 minBottoms golden, tops still pale
Cookie bars (11×7 dish)375°F (190°C)15–18 minToothpick comes out clean

Cookie bars baked in an 11×7 dish at 375°F for 15–18 minutes follow University of Illinois Extension, and cut-out (rolled) cookies at 375°F for 8–10 minutes match University of Wyoming Extension's "Baking It Up!". The 350°F (175°C) standard for chocolate chip, oatmeal, and drop sugar cookies is the published convention across home-baking references and university extension recipes.

Method: how to bake cookies, step by step

1. Preheat fully. Wait until the oven reaches temperature before the dough goes in — a cold start makes cookies spread flat. 2. Line the pan. Use parchment or a silicone mat; greasing the pan promotes spreading. 3. Space the dough. Leave at least 2 inches between portions so the cookies have room to spread. 4. Bake one sheet at a time on the middle rack for even heat; if you must bake two, swap and rotate them halfway through. 5. Pull early. Take the sheet out when the edges are set but the centers still look wet — they finish setting as they cool on the pan for 2 minutes, then move to a wire rack.

While the oven preheats you can launch any kitchen countdown — the same timer you'd use to bake a potato works for a sheet of cookies.

Variables that change the bake time

Several factors move a cookie out of the chart's range, and you should set the timer accordingly:

  • Dough temperature. Warm dough spreads fast and bakes thin in 8–9 minutes; chilled dough holds its shape and may need 11–12. The FDA recommends refrigerating cookie dough at 40°F or below, so dough straight from the fridge always bakes slower than room-temperature dough.
  • Cookie size. A 1-tbsp cookie finishes 2–3 minutes before a 3-tbsp one. Portion with a scoop so every cookie bakes the same.
  • Sheet color. Dark sheets overbrown the bottom; Colorado State University Extension notes that a dark pan can scorch cookies and recommends parchment or a lighter sheet.
  • Oven accuracy. Home ovens routinely run 25°F hot or cold. CSU Extension's food-safety specialists advise checking the dial against an oven thermometer before you trust it.
  • Altitude. Above 3,000 feet, CSU Extension recommends increasing the oven temperature by no more than 25°F and shortening the bake time to keep cookies from spreading.

Food safety: raw flour and eggs

Cookie dough is a raw food. Flour is a raw agricultural product that can carry Salmonella and pathogenic E. coli, and most homemade dough also contains raw eggs. The FDA states plainly that cooking is the only way to be sure foods made with flour and raw eggs are safe, that you should never eat raw dough or batter — and the agency explicitly warns against trying to heat-treat flour at home, since home methods may not kill all the bacteria.

Because most cookies contain eggs, the safe-cooking benchmark for egg dishes applies: USDA FSIS sets 160°F (71.1°C) as the safe minimum internal temperature for eggs and egg dishes. A thin cookie baked until its edges are golden and its surface is set reaches that temperature easily, which is why a fully baked cookie is safe to eat while the raw dough it came from is not. For styles that stay wet in the middle — gooey cookie bars or skillet cookies — the USDA's egg guidance says to verify 160°F in the center with a food thermometer.

Troubleshooting common cookie problems

Cookies spread into one puddle: the dough was too warm, the pan was greased, or the oven ran cool. Chill the dough 30 minutes, switch to parchment, and verify the temperature. Raw centers, burnt edges: the oven runs hot or the cookies are oversized — lower the temp 25°F and portion smaller. Hard, dry cookies: you baked past doneness; pull when centers still look slightly underdone. Pale, cakey cookies: too much flour — spoon flour into the cup and level it off rather than scooping. Uneven baking across the sheet: rotate the pan halfway through.

How to tell when cookies are done

Visual cues beat the clock. A drop cookie is done when the edges are firm and lightly golden and a 1-inch circle in the center still looks wet and puffy — it will set as it cools. Cut-out cookies are done when the edges just begin to color but the surface is still pale; shortbread when the bottoms are golden. For cookie bars and any thick or gooey style, confirm with a thermometer: 160°F in the center verifies both doneness and egg safety.

guides.title: How Long to Cook Oatmeal (Rolled, Steel-Cut & Microwave)
guides.excerpt: Rolled oatmeal takes ~5 minutes stovetop (2½–3 microwaved), quick oats 1 minute, steel-cut 15–30 minutes. Times and food-safety rules verified from Quaker, USDA FSIS, and university extensions.
guides.content:
By Suraj Giri, researcher at The Blog Timer. Updated 2026-08-09.

How long does oatmeal take to cook?

Cook rolled (old-fashioned) oatmeal about 5 minutes on the stovetop or 2½ to 3 minutes in the microwave; quick oats need about 1 minute on the stove; and steel-cut oats take 15 to 30 minutes of gentle simmering, depending on the cut. Instant oatmeal simply stands 2 minutes in hot liquid. These times come from Quaker's preparation guide and recipes from Oregon State University Extension.

Cooking times by oat type

The four shelf staples — instant, quick, rolled, and steel-cut — are the same grain milled to different sizes, so the main thing that changes is how long water takes to penetrate them. Use this table as a starting point; all ratios are liquid-to-oats by volume.

Oat typeLiquid : oatsStovetopMicrowave
Instant (precooked)~¾ cup : ½ cupStand 2 min in hot liquid60–75 sec (HIGH)
Quick (1-minute)1 cup : ½ cup~1 min1½–2 min (HIGH)
Rolled (old-fashioned)1 cup : ½ cup~5 min2½–3 min (HIGH)
Steel-cut (traditional)2¼–3 cups : 1 cup15–30 min simmer2½–3 min at 50% power (quick-cut only)

The figures above match Quaker's official directions for packaged oats, cross-checked against the University of Missouri Extension oats publication, which notes a standard ratio of roughly two cups of liquid to one cup of oats for rolled and quick varieties.

How to cook rolled oats on the stovetop

For one serving, bring 1 cup of water or milk to a rolling boil with a pinch of salt, then stir in ½ cup of rolled oats. Reduce the heat to medium and cook about 5 minutes (per Quaker's old-fashioned stovetop directions), stirring occasionally — set a 5-minute timer for standard texture. For a softer, creamier bowl, simmer up to 10 minutes instead (a 10-minute timer catches it before it turns to paste). The pinch of salt matters more than people think: Missouri Extension specifically notes it "brings out a nutty oat flavor" rather than making the cereal taste salty.

How to cook steel-cut oats

Steel-cut oats are whole groats chopped into gritty pieces, so they need real simmer time. Bring 3 cups of water to a boil, add 1 cup of oats, reduce to low, and simmer uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring a few times; then let the pot stand 2 minutes off the heat before serving, per the Oregon State University Extension recipe. Quaker's own steel-cut instructions run a little longer — 25 to 30 minutes for the traditional cut — so set a 30-minute timer if you like them fully tender. Pre-soaking the groats overnight, or toasting them briefly in butter before adding liquid, shaves several minutes off and deepens the flavor.

Microwave oatmeal when you're short on time

The microwave is the fastest path for rolled and quick oats. Combine ½ cup of rolled oats with about 1 cup of liquid in a large microwave-safe bowl (use one bigger than you think you need — oatmeal climbs the walls as it foams) and heat on HIGH for 2½ to 3 minutes, stirring once halfway. Quick oats take 1½ to 2 minutes, per Quaker's microwave directions. Milk-based oatmeal foams more than water-based, so drop the power to 70% or pause to stir if it threatens to overflow.

Variables that change the cooking time

  • Liquid choice. Milk simmers near the same temperature as water but thickens the pot, so milk-based oatmeal can read "done" slightly earlier and creamier.
  • Altitude. Water boils at a lower temperature above 3,000 feet, so plan on extra simmer time — a little longer for rolled oats and several minutes more for steel-cut.
  • Cut and freshness. Older oats can be drier and need an extra splash of liquid; freshly milled steel-cut cook a minute or two faster.
  • Soaking. An overnight soak in water or milk can cut steel-cut morning cook time roughly in half.

If you also cook other breakfast grains, the ratios and reasoning carry over to our quinoa timing guide and rice timing guide.

Food safety and leftovers

Dry oats are a low-moisture shelf-stable good, so the safety risk is in how you handle the cooked pot, not the raw grain. Cool and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours of cooking — the window Missouri Extension states in its recipe notes. The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service supplies the underlying rule: bacteria multiply fastest in the "danger zone" between 40°F and 140°F, cooked leftovers keep 3 to 4 days in the refrigerator, and frozen oatmeal stays safe 3 to 4 months. Reheat leftover oatmeal until it steams throughout (165°F), and if you cook it with eggs or dairy, treat the bowl like any other perishable — never leave it on the counter.

Troubleshooting common oatmeal problems

  • Gummy or paste-like: too little liquid or heat that's too high. Cook at a simmer, not a boil, and start at the 1-cup-liquid-to-½-cup-oats ratio.
  • Bland: almost always missing salt. Add the pinch before the oats hit the water, not after.
  • Crunchy steel-cut: undercooked or under-liquid. Add ¼ cup of hot water and simmer another 3–5 minutes.
  • Boils over in the microwave: the bowl is too small or the power too high. Use a deeper bowl and drop to 70% power.
